   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From Bill Clark, CUMBRIA

Thank you for printing my letter
in the February issue.

Regarding your answer about how
to put a bootblock on a blank
disc (ie, LOAD "*"), you said
refer to a page in the +3 manual
but I must point out that I know
nothing about machine code and
when I looked in the manual it
just looked a load of nonsense
to me. Could you please print
how to write a BASIC routine to
load these funny numbers and
letters and tell me step by step
how to enter it?

Could you tell me how you obtain
the text style print you use?


Are there any POKEs (and where
would I put them) to protect my
programs when listed.Is there a
POKE to cancel the protection so
I can update my programs?

How do you make your text
unreadable in your OUTLET issues
(ie, try listing).If the program
is RUN again, the text is O.K.
What is the routine for this?

I also have a problem with a
disk which is not very old and
has only been used a few times.
When LOADed or CATed it comes up
with an error "UNRECOGNIZED DISK
FORMAT". I've tried typing
"FORMAT A:" but I still get the
same error report and I can't
format it. Can I cure this?


Is there any way of getting more
than 58K from Drive M?

Is there any way of getting more
than 64 files on a disk?

Please try to explain in simple
terms because I don't understand
machine code.

Are there any modem phone numb-
ers in use for the Spectrum +3?

I have an old +3 from which I
have salvaged the disc drive. Is
there a lead available and power
supply so I can connect it to my
other +3 and use as a B drive?

I am after a solution to the
adventure game"CUSTERD'S QUEST".


I have a 4 data teletext adaptor
and a Currah Micro Speech.I know
originally they were for 48K
hardware but can they work on a
+3 machine?


Please can you let me know the
date of the month I am expected
to receive OUTLET?


I've an Amstrad DMP2000 printer
and I need the dip switch sett-
ings as it won't produce graph-
ics all the time.

Also, when I try to print from
OUTLET using Tabloid mode, the
printer just prints a line or
two of rubbish then freezes up.


Special thanks to one of your
regular readers: Ron Smith of
London, N9 for all the help he
has given me.

         Best Regards,

          Bill Clark

Brian Cavers to Bill Clark

The bootstrap method described
in the +3 handbook is primarily
aimed at commercial machine code
developers so their machine code
programs can load automatically
and run without BASIC therefore
making it difficult to break in
and copy the program. I believe
it might be possible to get back
to BASIC but then you may as
well use a "DISK" file to boot.
Anyone else care to comment?

Our "text style" is AUTOCHARS
PLUS and is in most programs. If
you load LEAVER in this issue,
BREAK in and enter RUN 9990 then
enter 9994 then 9994 again it
will extract line 9994.....


Now, save it on a spare disc
with any name you like such as
"AUTOCHARS". Load your own pro-
gram, BREAK in and enter MERGE
"AUTOCHARS". At the start of
your own program put GO SUB 9994
and it will automatically create
the bold text when run. Remember
to resave your program and the
code within line 9994 will be
included.

The double-height text we use is
called DUBTEX. REload LEAVER and
BREAK and RUN 9990 but this time
enter 9995 and then 9996 to get
DUBTEX isolated. Again, save it
as say, "DUBTEX" and merge it in
your own programs. Put a GO SUB
9995 at the start of your prog-
ram...


Now, to switch to double height
text just use...

PRINT USR D;"text" etc.

To restore to normal use...

PRINT USR S;"text".

You only need to use each one
ONCE. That is, once you have one
line that says PRINT USR D all
the remaining text you print
will be double height until you
either use USR S or clear the
screen with CLS. You can mix it
to, eg, PRINT USR D;"ONE";USR S;
"TWO";USR D" etc. I recommend
you end with USR S. You don't
need to actually print anything,
eg, PRINT USR D;"TEXT";USR S


Our "unreadable" text is not an
intended feature of OUTLET but
rather a design flaw of 128K
BASIC. We mostly have a routine
at line 9900 to STOP the problem
but sometimes there is not room.
It is caused by having a new
character set installed (such as
AUTOCHARS) at a position in mem-
ory higher than 49152. This will
work fine when a program is
running but when you stop it in
128K mode, the memory from 49152
to 65535 is paged out and the
page containing the 128K BASIC
editor is paged in. The system
variable at 23606 and 23607 has
the address of the current char
set; this still points above
49152 even though the char set
has been paged out...


Computers are pretty stupid;they
blindly follow instructions and
know now what they do. The Spec-
trum PRINT routine uses values
in memory which represent the
design of the text letters. If
these values are paged out and
something completely different
paged in it just blindly uses
the new values even if they are
meaningless and so prints total
garbage or just blanks. You can
get a similar effect if you just
POKE 23607 with any old number
from 0 to 255. The Spectrum will
then look in the wrong place for
the character designs.

Your bad disc is probably flawed
and unsaveable. You might try
formatting it with HIFORM (Issue
35).

I don't believe there is any way
to get more than 58K from the
RAM DISC with the existing hard-
ware.

I think it might be possible to
get more than 64 files on a +3
disc using a special format but
I don't know of one. This is yet
another reason why we cram most
of our code files into REM lines
so they all get saved as one
file.

There is no protection you can't
break given time. A simple one
is POKE 23659,0 but you can't
then use INPUT without restoring
it to normal with POKE 23659,2.
A BREAK disable method is better
but any fool can MERGE a program
to stop it.

There are more sophisticated
methods but you need to ask why
you need it. Why do you want to
stop people listing your prog-
rams?


It may be possible to use your
spare drive as a B drive. I have
heard that the power supply in
the +3 may be enough to run two
drives so if you open it up and
connect to the same place the
other drive is wired you may get
it to work. You will need to get
a CPC drive cable. Perhaps you
might see an advert in an Amst-
rad magazine? If you ever get to
any computer fairs you may pick
up a cable cheap or even a drive
with a PSU!


Your telext adaptor and Currah
Micro-Speech might work if you
get a FIXIT from BG SERVICES(see
OUTBOARD for address). However,
there are no promises. You might
even try them without. Again, it
is unlikely to do any damage but
the usual disclaimer - we cannot
accept responsibility for any
damage etc., etc! Naturally you
MUST switch off first if you
want to risk it.

Does anyone have any help for
the "CUSTERD'S QUEST" adventure?
It's not one I know.

You might try 4th dimension BB
on 0202 600 305 between 9pm and
6pm (the next day,ie NOT between
6pm and 9pm!).


You don't say what equipment you
are using but if you have a VTX
5000 then I'm told it will work
on the 4th dimension board else
send more info on your system.

Your printer problem does not
sound like a wrong dip switch
setting. Try switching OFF IBM
mode if there is one or NLQ. It
is hard to advise without seeing
the machine. When you say it
"does not produce graphics all
the time", please say exactly
what you are doing. It is more
likely you are sending the wrong
data. Is your +3 affected by the
infamouse +3 bug? If so, try the
POKEs given in J.D. Stringer's
letter in this issue and also in
last month too I think.
                         Brian

From Fred Ridout, SWINDON

Dear Ron,

Firstly, is it possible to
acquire a copy of the program
that puts the text into code for
reading on textloader?[text mode
on tape version - Ed] It seems
to me it would constitute the
basis for a memo program on a +2
because the recall on Textloader
is extremly fast and the index
in the first one or two pages
gives all the information
required to find a page quickly.

Secondly, I would like to know
if it is possible to find out
the amount of memory left on the
silicon disc on a +2?


Thirdly, is there any inform-
ation available on the extra
system variables in the +2?

          And oblige

          Fred Ridout

Brian Cavers to Fred Ridout

Our text viewer is probably not
suitable for general use. It was
done in a panic just before we
launched OUTLET in 1987 and has
not been altered since! It has
to have separate lines of BASIC
data set up to MERGE,it includes
the graphic headers special to
OUTLET, etc and it is rather
fiddly. The text has to be set
up especially with markers to
mark the end of each page - you
can't just load in any old Tas2
file! Some characters cannot be
used such as the tilde, curly
brackets, copyright,upright bar,
upright arrow etc. I'm used to
it but I think most people would
find it hard to come to grips
with it.

If you want to create memos from
scratch it is far easier and
just as fast to use the BASIC
PRINT. How about...

 10 LET PAGE = 1
 50 GO SUB PAGE * 100
 60 print prompt bar
 70 PAUSE
 80 lines to get keypress
 90 GO TO 50

100 PRINT ......"page 1"
199 RETURN

200 PRINT.....  "page 2
299 RETURN

If you need any help write again
but it depends just exactly what
you want and how you plan to use
it.

I've only got system variables
for the +3. Someone is going to
send me a photocopy of the +2
system variables from the manual
so I'll put them in a future
issue.

Apparently, there is a method of
PEEKing these system variables
and working out the amount of
space left in the RAM disc. If
I find out I will let you know.

If you like dabbling what I
would do if I were you is set up
a program to display the sysvars
then try saving and erasing a
file of known length and looking
to see which sysvars change and
how.
                        Brian

From J.D. Stringer, SHEFFIELD


Dear Editors,

        Re: +3 Printing

It might be worth repeating in
OUTLET how two common printing
problems can be resolved.

If the Centronics printer will
do no more than "COPY" then the
following should activate it :-

 POKE 23354,62:POKE 23355,16:NEW

The line must be written in the
correct sequence. The NEW is
important but do NOT then reset
the computer!


 Once the printer is operating
 correctly,double spacing
 between printed lines can be
 avoided by halving each line
 feed with this or similar
 Basic:-

FORMAT LPRINT "U":LPRINT CHR$ 27
;"A";CHR$ 6: FORMAT LPRINT "E"

Note the semicolons. Each line
feed then moves the paper by
6/72 inches rather than by the
default 12/72 inches associated
with six lines per inch (12/72 =
1/6).

         J.D Stringer

From Malcolm Goodman, Leeds.





Dear Brian/Ron,

In Issue 78 of Outlet there is a
query about mode switching
between 48K & 128K modes, to
which you replied that you were
not aware of any program that
would do this 'on the run'.


Perhaps if you looked at'TOGMOD'
or even '2 WAY SWITCH' (a copy
is enclosed on this disc) you
should find that one of them may
do the job.


Now on to SCREENMAKER that you
published in Issue 75, in which
I left out the part that allowed
the user to toggle between upper
and lower case on the two lower
screen lines and for which I in-
vited readers to try and provide
an answer.

Well, Miles Kinloch came up with
a reply that went some way to
resolving this puzzle, and you
went a step further in providing
an answer but I fail to
understand why the addition of..

305 PRINT ;

               ...in the program
provides a complete cure. Can
anyone offer a reason please?


Now on to printouts of selected
sections of OUTLETTERS.From time
to time there are queries and
answers to problems that are of
interest to me and which I would
like to copy to my printer using
(preferably) the TABLOID option.

I find however that I am unable
to just dump the required pages
to my printer without saving
every letter and replyu  to
paper. Is there some way that I
can just specify the page(s)
that I wish to LPRINT?

        Malcolm Goodman

Brian Cavers to Malcolm Goodman

I had no luck with "SWITCH". On
my +3 it correctly switched to
48K but when returning to 128K
it just set the screen black and
the keyboard locked up. This
happened on a 48K machine too
but intermittently; sometimes it
was the usr call and sometimes
the second. TOGMOD works but it
stops the program running. What
I want is something that can
load a program from +3 disc
(which MUST be in 128K mode as
the disc drive is not recognized
in 48K mode), switch to 48K to
run a program that only runs in
48K then switch back to 128K so
it can use the drive and return
to the rest of OUTLET.


As for the PRINT; mystery, it
must presumably change a flag in
a sysvar somewhere I guess. It
might be worth testing different
system variables before and
after to see?

You can print out a single page
of OUTLET text by pressing P but
not in TABLOID format of course.

                         Brian.

From Chris Ingram, MALAWI


Dear Outlet People,

I want to share a computing
experience I had yesterday and
see if any suggestions can be
offered.

Using my grey +2 in 48K mode
with Disciple and 3.5" double
disc drive attached, I sat down
for a lengthy session with Mast-
erfile 09 updating and adding to
a file. After each batch of
entries I saved the program (MM
V P) alternately to each drive.
At the end I saved onto a couple
more discs that I had also used
a few times at the beginning.


My troubles began after all this
when I went to use the Master-
file discs with another file and
found that the Autoload program
had been corrupted. Trying the
other discs I found first that
the Masterfile machine code was
corrupt, then the file I wanted
to load refused to do so. Some
of the messages I was getting
were: Invalid Filename, End of
File,Statement End Error,Invalid
Colour, Variable not found or
just a plain seize-up.


When I ran the discs through a
sector-checker I was alarmed
when up to half the files on all
four discs were corrupt (either
too many or not enough sectors).


Fortunately it wasn't the same
files on each disc so I was able
to spend an hour or two erasing
the corrupt ones and resaving
them from another disc


However,my faith in the Disciple
took quite a bashing. These are
discs that I use every day con-
taining some of my hardworking
Masterfile programs so I'm sure
the files weren't corrupt
already.

Can your boffins provide any
explanation for this? Is there
anything I can do to prevent it
happening again or at least stop
it before too much damage is
done?


While I was updating the first
file nothing suspicious happened
- no sector errors or hang-ups -
and that particular file was not
corrupted by itself (or at least
the last two saves were all
right).

        Yours sincerely,

         Chris Ingram

Brian Cavers to Chris Ingram

I was worried when I heard this
and rather perplexed. The sympt-
oms are exactly the same that I
had on my +D which was cured in
the end by switching to Betados.

It does not seem strange that
the Disciple might show the same
problem, after all, the DOS has
the same origins, what is weird
is why doesn't this happen on a
regular basis to everybody?

I suspect it is most common on
discs with rather a lot of files
and when one loads a file,alters
it and resaves it - perhaps with
no erase but just answering YES
to the OVERWRITE? prompt.


Possibly the system does not do
the right tests in such a situ-
ation. The worst of it is,if you
methodically do a back up disc
of the disc you are working on
and then save the file on both
disc then BOTH discs may be
corrupted! The discs may vary
slightly and so the corruption
may vary slightly.

We have had several mods to DOS
sent in recently which I have
not digested yet but they may
help though it will take a while
before they get published in
OUTLET.

Meanwhile,I can only suggest you
do TWO back up discs for import-
ant files, each containing only
half the master disc.

Furthermore,if you come to alter
a file and resave it then it may
help to save it on the master
disc and then on a tempory disc
that is not very full. Now check
the main disc is still OK. If it
is, copy the changed file from
the temporary disc to the back
up disc. If, however, the main
disc has become corrupted, at
least you have the back up to
recreate it plus a copy of the
latest file.

This is not very encouraging but
I am only speaking of really
crucial data where you have a
real fear of loss. I have been
in the position where the OUTLET
master and two backups were ALL
corrupted (in different parts)!
                        Brian

From Chris Oliver, STAFFS


Some questions were asked by
Fred Ridout in OUTLETTERS in the
February issue about monitors
which prompted Brian Cavers to
enquire about what types of
monitors people are using. Well,
speaking for myself, it's
sometimes useful when editing
programs to have two systems
running concurrently, so here
are details of the two that I
use, in age order, eldest first:


1) A Philips CM8524 Monitor
running on an original 48k
Spectrum, with a nice Saga key-
board.


This monitor will accept TTL-RGB
but unfortunately not with
BRIGHT ("RGB" simply stands for
Red-Green-Blue. ie. separate
signals are sent on three
separate lines to the 3 colour
guns in the tube).

It also accepts composite video
signals, and BRIGHT is accept-
able in this mode. (Composite
Video scrambles all the signals
together and sends them down one
line to be unscrambled in the
monitor.

It gives a picture which is a
big improvement on a Spectrum
screen sent to a television, but
tends to suffer from "dot-crawl"
and is not as clear as the RGB
system).

As it is not easy to obtain the
separate RGB signals from the
original Spectrum, I have tapped
into the composite video signal
before it goes into the TV modu-
lator and this goes straight to
the monitor's composite video
input. There have been articles
in OUTLET in the past on just
where to make the connections.

The Philips monitor has a built-
in sound amplifier so I have
also run a wire from the EAR
socket on the Spectrum to the
monitor's sound input socket.

2) An Amstrad CTM 644 Monitor
running on a 128 grey-cased +2.
This gives an excellent clear
rock-steady RGB picture and does
support BRIGHT.

One small snag is that it has no
sound amplifier but this is
easily overcome by sending the
128 sound output to any spare
audio amplifier. eg. a cassette
player, radio, or record player.


There are still second-hand CTM
644s or even some brand new ones
to be had. Try Micro Mart, or as
Malcolm Perry suggests, Radio
Fairs are a good source. They
were selling last year ('93) at
`70 to `80 each.


You will need a lead to connect
from the 8-pin DIN socket on the
+2 to the 6-pin DIN plug on the
monitor...


Note that the numbering convent-
ion on each of these "standard"
DIN connectors is quite differ-
ent but with luck, the number of
each pin will be marked on the
inside of the connector.Once you
have determined which is which,
the connections need to be made
as follows:-
   SPECTRUM           MONITOR
 9-pin socket        6-pin plug

Pin 2 = Zero Volts    = Pin 5

Pin 5 = Vertical sync = Pin 4

Pin 6 = Green         = Pin 1

Pin 7 = Red           = Pin 2

Pin 8 = Blue          = Pin 3


One small but very worthwhile
extra refinement, is to add in a
small preset variable resistor
into each of the three colour
lines. These are tiny wafer-thin
thingys which you twiddle [these
technical terms leave me totally
awestruck - BC] with a small
screwdriver to alter each colour
intensity until the optimum
colour balance is reached.


This is all that is required
with the +2, but Malcolm Perry
describes other refinements to
match the SAM etc in his
DRIVECHAT in Issue 61 and in his
letter in Issue 75.



Incidentally, "TTL" stands for
"transistor-transistor logic",
which is a type of electronic
digital switching circuitry most
suited to black-and-white images
with no in-between levels. So it
would appear that the +2 manual
is not correct when it refers to
TTL in conjunction with the RGB,
as BRIGHT is present on the RGB
lines.

If you get into difficulties,
drop us a line at OUTLET.

            Cheers,

              Chris

From Les Tyler, CHELTENHAM

I note references to an improved
CATLOADER 2. I would like to
modify my copy to accept the
enhanced number of files avail-
able with BETADOS. Will the new
version take more than 80 files
or any chance of a mod to allow
this, please? I use CATLOADER 2
extensively so this would be a
most useful update.

Is it possible to include CODE
start addresses and file lengths
in those OUTLET programs that
call such files, e.g., the
various demos, etc.? I like to
back all programs up to tape and
it would be helpful to include
this information in line 9983.


As it is, one has to CAT the
OUTLET disc to determine whether
or not there is CODE or DATA in
addition to the BASIC.


Long-term subscribers to OUTLET
may recall that a couple of
years or so ago I had a letter
featured that dealt with sector
errors and the beneficial effect
that my UNIDOS-fitted DISCIPLE
had on occasions, i.e. it
appeared to ignore these errors
when copying from one disc to
another. I have not uncovered
anything since that disputed
these findings and think that it
might be a good idea to remind
UNIDOS holders of the possibil-
ities.


I no longer have a DISCIPLE
myself and have not fitted the
+D with UNIDOS but reading the
BETADOS manual suggests there
may be a possible alternative...

Where errors occur in the DIR-
ECTORY tracks, I normally find
that some or all of the disc is
unusable, although there are
exceptions, say when you know
the actual file number and can
LOAD Pn;this works on occasions.
From Page 4 of the BETADOS
manual I get the impression that
provided there is no actual
physical damage it should be
possible to overwrite the entire
DIRECTORY area with a back-up
copy saved on the disc as a
normal CODE file.


I have tried this, and it works
OK on an uncorrupted disc, I do
not have one with sector errors
in this area at the moment,
(neither do I want any !), so
can't check on that, but would
welcome any comments.

Perhaps I'm trying to do the
impossible, but it looks worth a
try!
            Cheers!

              Les

Brian Cavers to Les Tyler

Sorry, Les. There are no plans
to modify CATLOADER 2 further at
present. It would need an exten-
sive re-write to get it do more
than 80 files. The BASIC just
squeezes in below the code.If an
extra page of 40 files or more
was added it simply would not
fit at present. In any change,
the copy and text view routines
would have to be reduced. In any
event, it might involve weeks or
months of work and the market
for such a need is very small
(probably about one man actually
- you!). Find me 7,000 buyers or
alternatively, give me `7,000 -
and I'll try it; no promises
mind you.


Line 9983 is used during conver-
sion from +D to tape and +3(that
is why there is a funny bit on
the end of line 9983) so code
saves cannot go on the end. In
addition, many files change on
loading so cannot be saved and
some load other files at other
times.

There is no easy solution. We
might just put the simple ones
where there is just code at say
line 9976 in tape syntax so +3
users could also use it and +D
users could easily alter the
syntax I suppose. I'll pass a
note to our programs editor,
Chris Oliver, but I'm not sure
of a good solution.
                    Brian

Brian Cavers to Bill Clark

The bootstrap method described in the +3 handbook is primarily aimed at commercial machine code developers so their machine code programs can load automatically and run without BASIC therefore making it difficult to break in and copy the program. I believe it might be possible to get back to BASIC but then you may as well use a "DISK" file to boot. Anyone else care to comment?

Our "text style" is AUTOCHARS PLUS and is in most programs. If you load LEAVER in this issue, BREAK in and enter RUN 9990 then enter 9994 then 9994 again it will extract line 9994.....

Now, save it on a spare disc with any name you like such as "AUTOCHARS". Load your own pro- gram, BREAK in and enter MERGE "AUTOCHARS". At the start of your own program put GO SUB 9994 and it will automatically create the bold text when run. Remember to resave your program and the code within line 9994 will be included.

The double-height text we use is called DUBTEX. REload LEAVER and BREAK and RUN 9990 but this time enter 9995 and then 9996 to get DUBTEX isolated. Again, save it as say, "DUBTEX" and merge it in your own programs. Put a GO SUB 9995 at the start of your prog- ram...

Now, to switch to double height text just use...

PRINT USR D;"text" etc.

To restore to normal use...

PRINT USR S;"text".

You only need to use each one ONCE. That is, once you have one line that says PRINT USR D all the remaining text you print will be double height until you either use USR S or clear the screen with CLS. You can mix it to, eg, PRINT USR D;"ONE";USR S; "TWO";USR D" etc. I recommend you end with USR S. You don't need to actually print anything, eg, PRINT USR D;"TEXT";USR S

Our "unreadable" text is not an intended feature of OUTLET but rather a design flaw of 128K BASIC. We mostly have a routine at line 9900 to STOP the problem but sometimes there is not room. It is caused by having a new character set installed (such as AUTOCHARS) at a position in mem- ory higher than 49152. This will work fine when a program is running but when you stop it in 128K mode, the memory from 49152 to 65535 is paged out and the page containing the 128K BASIC editor is paged in. The system variable at 23606 and 23607 has the address of the current char set; this still points above 49152 even though the char set has been paged out...

Computers are pretty stupid;they blindly follow instructions and know now what they do. The Spec- trum PRINT routine uses values in memory which represent the design of the text letters. If these values are paged out and something completely different paged in it just blindly uses the new values even if they are meaningless and so prints total garbage or just blanks. You can get a similar effect if you just POKE 23607 with any old number from 0 to 255. The Spectrum will then look in the wrong place for the character designs.

Your bad disc is probably flawed and unsaveable. You might try formatting it with HIFORM (Issue 35).

I don't believe there is any way to get more than 58K from the RAM DISC with the existing hard- ware.

I think it might be possible to get more than 64 files on a +3 disc using a special format but I don't know of one. This is yet another reason why we cram most of our code files into REM lines so they all get saved as one file.

There is no protection you can't break given time. A simple one is POKE 23659,0 but you can't then use INPUT without restoring it to normal with POKE 23659,2. A BREAK disable method is better but any fool can MERGE a program to stop it.

There are more sophisticated methods but you need to ask why you need it. Why do you want to stop people listing your prog- rams?

It may be possible to use your spare drive as a B drive. I have heard that the power supply in the +3 may be enough to run two drives so if you open it up and connect to the same place the other drive is wired you may get it to work. You will need to get a CPC drive cable. Perhaps you might see an advert in an Amst- rad magazine? If you ever get to any computer fairs you may pick up a cable cheap or even a drive with a PSU!

Your telext adaptor and Currah Micro-Speech might work if you get a FIXIT from BG SERVICES(see OUTBOARD for address). However, there are no promises. You might even try them without. Again, it is unlikely to do any damage but the usual disclaimer - we cannot accept responsibility for any damage etc., etc! Naturally you MUST switch off first if you want to risk it.

Does anyone have any help for the "CUSTERD'S QUEST" adventure? It's not one I know.

You might try 4th dimension BB on 0202 600 305 between 9pm and 6pm (the next day,ie NOT between 6pm and 9pm!).

You don't say what equipment you are using but if you have a VTX 5000 then I'm told it will work on the 4th dimension board else send more info on your system.

Your printer problem does not sound like a wrong dip switch setting. Try switching OFF IBM mode if there is one or NLQ. It is hard to advise without seeing the machine. Some questions were asked by Fred Ridout in OUTLETTERS in the February issue about monitors which prompted Brian Cavers to enquire about what types of monitors people are using. 1) A Philips CM8524 Monitor running on an original 48k Spectrum, with a nice Saga key- board.

This monitor will accept TTL-RGB but unfortunately not with BRIGHT ("RGB" simply stands for Red-Green-Blue. ie. separate signals are sent on three separate lines to the 3 colour guns in the tube).

It also accepts composite video signals, and BRIGHT is accept- able in this mode. (Composite Video scrambles all the signals together and sends them down one line to be unscrambled in the monitor.

It gives a picture which is a big improvement on a Spectrum screen sent to a television, but tends to suffer from "dot-crawl" and is not as clear as the RGB system).

As it is not easy to obtain the separate RGB signals from the original Spectrum, I have tapped into the composite video signal before it goes into the TV modu- lator and this goes straight to the monitor's composite video input. There have been articles in OUTLET in the past on just where to make the connections.

The Philips monitor has a built- in sound amplifier so I have also run a wire from the EAR socket on the Spectrum to the monitor's sound input socket.

2) An Amstrad CTM 644 Monitor running on a 128 grey-cased +2. This gives an excellent clear rock-steady RGB picture and does support BRIGHT.

One small snag is that it has no sound amplifier but this is easily overcome by sending the 128 sound output to any spare audio amplifier. eg. a cassette player, radio, or record player.

There are still second-hand CTM 644s or even some brand new ones to be had. Try Micro Mart, or as Malcolm Perry suggests, Radio Fairs are a good source. They were selling last year ('93) at `70 to `80 each.

You will need a lead to connect from the 8-pin DIN socket on the +2 to the 6-pin DIN plug on the monitor...

Note that the numbering convent- ion on each of these "standard" DIN connectors is quite differ- ent but with luck, the number of each pin will be marked on the inside of the connector.Once you have determined which is which, the connections need to be made as follows:- SPECTRUM           MONITOR 9-pin socket        6-pin plug

Pin 2 = Zero Volts    = Pin 5

Pin 5 = Vertical sync = Pin 4

Pin 6 = Green         = Pin 1

Pin 7 = Red           = Pin 2

Pin 8 = Blue          = Pin 3

One small but very worthwhile extra refinement, is to add in a small preset variable resistor into each of the three colour lines. These are tiny wafer-thin thingys which you twiddle [these technical terms leave me totally awestruck - BC] with a small screwdriver to alter each colour intensity until the optimum colour balance is reached.

This is all that is required with the +2, but Malcolm Perry describes other refinements to match the SAM etc in his DRIVECHAT in Issue 61 and in his letter in Issue 75.

Incidentally, "TTL" stands for "transistor-transistor logic", which is a type of electronic digital switching circuitry most suited to black-and-white images with no in-between levels. So it would appear that the +2 manual is not correct when it refers to TTL in conjunction with the RGB, as BRIGHT is present on the RGB lines.

If you get into difficulties, drop us a line at OUTLET.

Chris

Не забудьте пересохранить вашу программу, и код внутри строки 9994 будет сохранен вместе с ней.

Он также принимает композитный видеосигнал, и в этом режиме BRIGHT поддерживается. (Композитное видео смешивает все сигналы вместе и посылает их по одному проводу для последующего разделения в мониторе. Картинка получается намного лучше, чем при подключении Spectrum к телевизору, но страдает эффектом «бегущих точек» (dot-crawl) и уступает по четкости системе RGB).

Поскольку получить раздельные RGB-сигналы от оригинального Spectrum непросто, я взял композитный видеосигнал до того, как он поступает на ТВ-модулятор, и вывел его прямо на композитный видеовход монитора. В прошлых номерах OUTLET были статьи о том, где именно нужно припаиваться.

У монитора Philips есть встроенный звуковой усилитель, поэтому я также протянул провод от гнезда EAR на Spectrum к звуковому входу монитора.

2) Монитор Amstrad CTM 644, работающий с серым 128 +2. Он дает превосходную, четкую, стабильную как скала RGB-картинку и поддерживает BRIGHT.

Один небольшой минус — в нем нет звукового усилителя, но это легко решить, подав аудиовыход со 128 на любой свободный усилитель (например, магнитофон, радиоприемник или проигрыватель пластинок).

Подержанные CTM 644 (или даже совершенно новые) все еще можно найти. Попробуйте поискать в Micro Mart или, как советует Malcolm Perry, на радиоярмарках. В прошлом году ('93) они продавались по £70–£80 за штуку.

Вам понадобится кабель для подключения 8-контактного разъема DIN на +2 к 6-контактному штекеру DIN на мониторе...

Обратите внимание, что нумерация контактов у этих «стандартных» разъемов DIN совершенно разная, но, если повезет, номер каждого контакта будет выбит на внутренней стороне разъема. Как только вы определите, какой где, соединения выполняются следующим образом:

```text
   SPECTRUM               МОНИТОР
8-контактное гнездо   6-контактный штекер

Pin 2 = 0 Вольт     = Pin 5
Pin 5 = Кадровая    = Pin 4
        синхронизация
Pin 6 = Green       = Pin 1
Pin 7 = Red         = Pin 2
Pin 8 = Blue        = Pin 3
```

Небольшая, но весьма полезная доработка — добавить небольшой подстроечный переменный резистор в каждую из трех цветовых линий. Это такие крошечные, тонкие, как вафля, штуковины, которые крутят [эти технические термины повергают меня в благоговейный трепет — BC] маленькой отверткой, регулируя интенсивность каждого цвета до достижения оптимального цветового баланса.

Это все, что требуется для +2, но Malcolm Perry описывает и другие тонкости (для согласования с SAM и т.д.) в своей рубрике DRIVECHAT в выпуске 61 и в письме в выпуске 75.

Кстати, «TTL» означает «транзисторно-транзисторная логика», которая представляет собой тип электронных цифровых схем переключения, наиболее подходящий для черно-белых изображений без промежуточных градаций. Поэтому руководство к +2, судя по всему, не совсем корректно, когда говорит о TTL применительно к RGB, поскольку сигнал BRIGHT присутствует на линиях RGB.
